column7: I buy fresh bread every morning.
column8: The kind of bread changes from country to country in Latin America: bolillo in Mexico, flauta in Argentina.

column6: Quiero un vaso de agua fría.
column7: I want a glass of cold water.
column8: Agua is feminine, but takes «el» in the singular because of the stress on the first syllable: el agua, but las aguas.

column6: La leche está en el refrigerador.
column7: The milk is in the fridge.
column8: «Leche» is feminine, but «mala leche» means bad temper or spite: a very common expression.

column6: Tomo un café antes de trabajar.
column7: I have a coffee before working.
column8: In Colombia and many other countries «tinto» means a small black coffee.

column6: Mi abuela bebe té todas las tardes.
column7: My grandmother drinks tea every afternoon.
column8: With the accent «té» is tea; without it «te» is a pronoun: you.

column6: Me gusta el jugo de naranja.
column7: I like orange juice.
column8: In Spain people say «zumo»; in Latin America almost everywhere it is «jugo».

column6: Mi padre prefiere el vino tinto.
column7: My father prefers red wine.
column8: In Spanish red wine is «tinto», not «rojo».

column7: We order a very cold beer.
column8: In many countries beer is ordered «bien helada» or «bien fría».

column7: I have an egg with bread for breakfast.
column8: In Mexico «huevos rancheros» are fried eggs with spicy sauce, a breakfast classic.

column6: Ella pone queso sobre la pizza.
column7: She puts cheese on the pizza.
column8: In Colombia and Venezuela «arepa con queso» is an everyday dish.

column7: I do not eat meat on Fridays.
column8: In Argentina the «asado» is a social ritual: the meat is grilled over embers for hours.

column7: Today I cook chicken with rice.
column8: «Pollo» means the meat; the live animal is «gallina», or «pollito» for a chick.

column6: Mi hermana come pescado los domingos.
column7: My sister eats fish on Sundays.
column8: Live fish is «pez», but fish on the plate is «pescado».

column6: El arroz es la base del plato.
column7: Rice is the base of the dish.
column8: An everyday food across Latin America: «arroz con frijoles» is the classic pair.

column6: Siempre llevo una fruta al trabajo.
column7: I always take a piece of fruit to work.
column8: «Fruta» is fruit in general or a single piece; «fruto» is the botanical fruit.

column6: La manzana roja está muy dulce.
column7: The red apple is very sweet.
column8: «Manzana» also means «city block» in many Latin American cities: «a dos manzanas de aquí».

column7: This orange has a lot of juice.
column8: «Naranja» is both the fruit and the colour; the tree is «naranjo».

column6: La sopa de pollo está caliente.
column7: The chicken soup is hot.
column8: In many countries lunch starts with a «sopa» before the main dish.

column7: I prefer a salad with tomatoes.
column8: «Ensalada» also appears as «ensaladilla» (Russian salad) in Spain.

column6: El desayuno es a las siete.
column7: Breakfast is at seven.
column8: The verb is «desayunar», from «des-» and «ayuno» (fast): to break the fast.

column6: El almuerzo está listo en casa.
column7: Lunch is ready at home.
column8: In Spain lunch is the main meal and is eaten late, around two or three.

column7: Dinner is with the family.
column8: In Latin America dinner is often lighter than lunch.

column7: I want to eat something tasty today.
column8: «Comer» also means «to have lunch»: in some countries «la comida» is the midday meal.

column6: Debo beber más agua al día.
column7: I must drink more water a day.
column8: In Mexico and elsewhere «tomar» is very common instead of «beber».

column6: Me encanta cocinar para mis amigos.
column7: I love cooking for my friends.
column8: «Cocinar» is the verb; «la cocina» is both the kitchen and a style of cooking.

column6: Voy a pedir la cuenta ahora.
column7: I am going to ask for the bill now.
column8: False friend: «pedir» is to ask for something, «preguntar» is to ask a question.

column6: La cuenta es de veinte dólares.
column7: The bill is twenty dollars.
column8: At a restaurant you ask «la cuenta, por favor»; in Spain a gesture to the waiter is often enough.

column7: I reserve a table for two.
column8: In Argentina and Uruguay «mesa» is also the restaurant table you book.

column6: El menú del día es barato.
column7: The set menu of the day is cheap.
column8: The «menú del día» is a fixed-price meal, very common in Spain and Latin America.

column6: La sopa está muy rica hoy.
column7: The soup is very tasty today.
column8: «Rico» also means rich: «una familia rica». Said of food it means tasty.

column7: My coffee is always sweet.
column8: «Dulce» is both an adjective and a noun: «un dulce» is a sweet treat.

column7: The coffee is very hot.
column8: For people say «tener calor», not «estar caliente», which means something else.

column7: The beer is very cold.
column8: For the weather say «hace frío»; for people «tener frío».

column7: This dish is very tasty.
column8: It is used mostly in Latin America; in Spain «rico» is preferred.

column7: It needs a little salt.
column8: «Sal» is feminine: «la sal». It is also the imperative of «salir»: «¡Sal de aquí!».

column6: No quiero azúcar en el café.
column7: I do not want sugar in my coffee.
column8: «Azúcar» can be masculine or feminine, but today «el azúcar» is almost always used.

column6: Mi casa está cerca del parque.
column7: My house is near the park.
column8: «En casa» means «at home»: «estoy en casa», «voy a casa».

column6: Mi cuarto es pequeño pero cómodo.
column7: My room is small but comfortable.
column8: In Latin America «cuarto» is the room; «habitación» is more common in Spain.

column6: La cocina tiene una ventana grande.
column7: The kitchen has a big window.
column8: The same word means the room and a style of cooking: «la cocina mexicana».

column6: El baño está al final del pasillo.
column7: The bathroom is at the end of the hall.
column8: The «ñ» is a letter of its own: «baño» (bathroom) is not «bano».

column7: Close the door, please.
column8: «Puerta» is also an airport gate: «puerta de embarque».

column7: The window looks onto the garden.
column8: «Ventana» comes from «viento» (wind): the window lets air in.

column7: My bed is very comfortable.
column8: «Cama» is the bed; «cama matrimonial» is the double bed.

column7: I need a taller chair.
column8: «Silla» is the chair; «sillón» is the armchair.

column6: El sofá es nuevo y grande.
column7: The sofa is new and big.
column8: It takes the accent on the last syllable: «sofá», plural «sofás».

column7: Where is the house key?
column8: «Llave» is also the tap in Latin America: «abrir la llave»; in Spain it is «grifo».

column7: My grandfather looks after the garden.
column8: «Jardín de infantes» is nursery school in Argentina.

column7: My family lives in Lima.
column8: The noun is singular: «mi familia vive», not «viven», even if many people.

column7: My mother cooks very well.
column8: «Mamá» is the affectionate form, used everywhere; «madre» is more formal.

column6: Mi padre trabaja en un banco.
column7: My father works in a bank.
column8: In the plural «los padres» are the parents, not only fathers.

column7: My brother is twelve years old.
column8: «Hermanos» can mean brothers and sisters together.

column7: Her son studies medicine.
column8: In the plural «los hijos» are the children, boys and girls.

column7: I want to live near the sea.
column8: «Vivir» means both to live and to dwell: «vivo en Roma».

column6: Voy a abrir la ventana ahora.
column7: I am going to open the window now.
column8: The past participle is irregular: «abierto».

column6: Voy a cerrar la puerta con llave.
column7: I am going to lock the door.
column8: The stem changes: «cierro, cierras, cierra» (e→ie).

column6: Hoy tengo que limpiar la casa.
column7: Today I have to clean the house.
column8: The adjective «limpio» is also used: «la cocina está limpia».

column7: I need to sleep eight hours a day.
column8: Irregular in the present: «duermo, duermes, duerme» (o→ue).

column7: I must wash the clothes today.
column8: «Lavarse» is to wash oneself: «me lavo las manos».

column6: Mi casa no es muy grande.
column7: My house is not very big.
column8: Before a singular noun it becomes «gran»: «un gran día».

column7: I live in a small town.
column8: «Chico» is very common in Latin America instead of «pequeño».

column7: We have a new sofa.
column8: It usually goes after the noun: «un sofá nuevo». It agrees: «nueva», «nuevos», «nuevas».

column7: This house is very old.
column8: For people «viejo» can offend: «mayor» is kinder.

column7: The kitchen is very clean.
column8: «Estar limpio» is clean right now; «ser limpio» describes a tidy person.

column7: This armchair is very comfortable.
column8: «Cómodo» works for things and people: «estoy cómodo».

column7: The hallway is very dark.
column8: «Oscuro» is also written «obscuro», but the short form is more common.

column7: I have a small house.
column8: It is also used for age: «tengo veinte años».

column6: El techo de mi cuarto es blanco.
column7: The ceiling of my room is white.
column8: «Techo» is both the roof and the inside ceiling.

column7: I live on the third floor.
column8: In Spain «piso» is the apartment; in Latin America it is the floor or storey.

column7: My neighbour plays the guitar.
column8: Feminine «vecina»; the neighbourhood is «el vecindario» or «el barrio».

column6: El viaje a Cusco dura una hora.
column7: The trip to Cusco takes an hour.
column8: To wish someone a good trip say «¡buen viaje!»; «viaje» is written with a «j».

column6: Mi ciudad tiene un río grande.
column7: My city has a big river.
column8: «Ciudad» ends in a consonant but is feminine: «la ciudad».

column7: My country has a lot of sun.
column8: The plural «países» keeps the accent on the «í».

column6: La calle está llena de gente.
column7: The street is full of people.
column8: In Latin America many streets are numbered: «calle 10» or «carrera 7» in Colombia.

column6: Nos vemos en la plaza central.
column7: We meet in the central square.
column8: Almost every Spanish-speaking town has a «Plaza Mayor» or «Plaza de Armas» at its centre.

column6: El tren sale a las nueve.
column7: The train leaves at nine.
column8: A loan from French «train»; the plural is «trenes».

column6: Tomo el autobús todos los días.
column7: I take the bus every day.
column8: It has many names: «camión» in Mexico, «colectivo» in Argentina, «guagua» in Cuba.

column6: El avión llega a las seis.
column7: The plane arrives at six.
column8: «Avión» is the plane; «aeropuerto» is the airport.

column7: My car is very old.
column8: In Spain people say «coche», in Argentina «auto»; «carro» is common in Mexico, Colombia, Peru.

column7: I buy a one-way ticket.
column8: In Latin America people usually say «boleto» or «pasaje»; «billete» is also a banknote.

column7: The hotel has a swimming pool.
column8: The «h» is silent: it is pronounced «otel».

column6: Necesito un mapa de la ciudad.
column7: I need a map of the city.
column8: It ends in «-a» but is masculine, like «día» and «problema».

column6: Mi maleta es azul y grande.
column7: My suitcase is blue and big.
column8: «Hacer la maleta» means to pack the suitcase.

column6: Vamos a la playa el domingo.
column7: We go to the beach on Sunday.
column8: «Playa» is the beach, not the sea: the sea is «el mar» (masculine). The coast is «la costa».

column6: Me gusta viajar con mi familia.
column7: I like to travel with my family.
column8: «Viajar» and «viaje» are written with «j».

column6: Siempre llego temprano a la estación.
column7: I always arrive early at the station.
column8: The «g» becomes «gu» before «e»: «llegué».

column6: El tren sale a las ocho.
column7: The train leaves at eight.
column8: False friend: «salir» is to go out or leave, not to go up (that is «subir»).

column6: Quiero ir a la playa mañana.
column7: I want to go to the beach tomorrow.
column8: «Ir a + infinitive» is the most common future: «voy a comer».

column7: Can you come to my house tomorrow?
column8: Irregular: «vengo, vienes, viene».

column6: Me gusta caminar por la ciudad.
column7: I like walking around the city.
column8: In Spain «andar» is more common; «caminar» dominates in Latin America.

column6: Voy a esperar el tren aquí.
column7: I am going to wait for the train here.
column8: One verb for both to wait and to hope: mind the context.

column7: I am looking for a quiet street.
column8: No preposition needed: «busco las llaves».

column7: I prefer to pay by card.
column8: You say «pagar algo» without a preposition: «pago la cuenta».

column6: Mi hotel está cerca del mar.
column7: My hotel is near the sea.
column8: It is used with «de»: «cerca de la plaza».

column6: Mi casa queda lejos del centro.
column7: My house is far from the centre.
column8: Opposite of «cerca»; used with «de»: «lejos de aquí».

column7: There is a good restaurant here.
column8: «Aquí» and «acá»: in Latin America «acá» is very common.

column7: My brother has lived there since 2020.
column8: There is also «allá», vaguer and farther away.

column6: El banco está a la derecha.
column7: The bank is on the right.
column8: You say «a la derecha» and «a la izquierda».

column7: Turn left here.
column8: «Gira», «dobla» or «voltea»: three verbs for turning, depending on the country.

column7: The station is very close.
column8: It also means «season»: «las cuatro estaciones».

column7: The airport is very modern.
column8: Do not mix up «puerto» (port) and «puerta» (door). At the airport there is «la puerta de embarque» (the gate).

column7: The train is very fast.
column8: As an adverb it stays the same: «habla rápido».

column7: The bus is too slow.
column8: Opposite of «rápido»; «despacio» is the adverb «slowly».

column7: The hotel is very cheap.
column8: Opposite: «caro». «Salir barato» means to work out cheap.

column6: Mi trabajo empieza a las ocho.
column7: My work starts at eight.
column8: «Trabajo» is work or a job: «buscar trabajo». The verb is «trabajar». «Empleo» is a formal word for employment.

column6: Mi oficina está en el centro.
column7: My office is in the city centre.
column8: «Oficina» is the office; «despacho» is a manager's room.

column7: My boss speaks three languages.
column8: For a woman you say «la jefa».

column6: Mi empresa vende ropa en línea.
column7: My company sells clothes online.
column8: «Empresa» is a business; «compañía» is more formal or international.

column6: La reunión es a las diez.
column7: The meeting is at ten.
column8: With events «ser» is used: «la reunión es a las diez».

column6: Trabajo con la computadora todo el día.
column7: I work on the computer all day.
column8: In Latin America «computadora» (Mexico, Argentina) or «computador» (Colombia, Chile).

column7: My phone rings very loudly.
column8: The mobile is «el celular» in Latin America and «el móvil» in Spain.

column7: I check my mail every morning.
column8: «Correo» is mail; «correo electrónico» is email.

column6: Tenemos un problema con el correo.
column7: We have a problem with the mail.
column8: It ends in «-a» but is masculine: «el problema».

column7: I have no cash on me.
column8: It is not used in the plural: «mucho dinero».

column7: Every employee has their own desk.
column8: Feminine: «la empleada».

column6: El escritorio está lleno de papeles.
column7: The desk is full of papers.
column8: The desk is the office desk.

column7: I am going to work from home.
column8: «Trabajar de» + profession: «trabaja de cocinero».

column7: We need to talk to the boss.
column8: It takes no preposition: «necesito ayuda».

column7: Can you talk to the client?
column8: The «h» is silent: «hablar» sounds like «ablar».

column7: I always help my colleagues.
column8: «Ayuda» is the noun: «necesito ayuda».

column7: I have to write an email.
column8: Irregular participle: «escrito».

column7: I like to read the newspaper.
column8: The past «leyó» has a «y» because two vowels meet.

column6: Voy a llamar a mi jefe.
column7: I am going to call my boss.
column8: «Llamarse» is to be called: «me llamo Ana».

column6: Quiero ganar más dinero este año.
column7: I want to earn more money this year.
column8: One verb for earning and winning: «ganar un partido».

column6: La clase va a empezar ahora.
column7: The class is about to begin now.
column8: The stem changes: «empiezo» (e→ie).

column6: Voy a terminar el informe hoy.
column7: I am going to finish the report today.
column8: «Acabar» is a very frequent synonym.

column7: This meeting is very important.
column8: The same in masculine and feminine: «un día importante».

column6: Mi jefe está muy ocupado hoy.
column7: My boss is very busy today.
column8: With «estar» it shows a state: «estoy ocupado».

column7: The exam is very difficult.
column8: Opposite: «fácil». The plural is «difíciles».

column7: This job is not easy.
column8: The adverb is «fácilmente».

column6: Mi madre está muy cansada hoy.
column7: My mother is very tired today.
column8: With «estar» it shows a state of tiredness right now.

column7: The teacher explains the lesson.
column8: Feminine: «la profesora».

column6: Mi hermana es estudiante de medicina.
column7: My sister is a medicine student.
column8: The same in masculine and feminine: «el/la estudiante».

column6: Mi tío es doctor en física.
column7: My uncle has a doctorate in physics.
column8: Feminine: «la doctora»; «médico» is the profession of physician.

column7: The client wants to talk to you.
column8: The same in masculine and feminine: «el/la cliente».

column6: La tienda abre a las nueve.
column7: The shop opens at nine.
column8: «Tienda» is the shop; «tienda de campaña» is the camping tent.

column7: I buy vegetables at the market.
column8: «El mercado» is the market; the supermarket is «el supermercado». Also «mercado laboral» (job market).

column6: El precio de la camisa es bajo.
column7: The price of the shirt is low.
column8: You say «un precio bajo/alto», not small/big.

column7: I want to buy new clothes.
column8: «Ropa» is a collective singular: «la ropa está limpia».

column7: This shirt is made of cotton.
column8: It is not the «camiseta» (T-shirt), which is more casual.

column7: I need a bigger shoe.
column8: It is usually used in the plural: «unos zapatos».

column7: I carry a cloth bag.
column8: In Mexico it is also a shopping bag; in Spain «bolso» is the handbag.

column6: Busco un regalo para mi madre.
column7: I am looking for a gift for my mother.
column8: «Regalar» is to give as a gift; «dar» is simply to give.

column7: I pay with a credit card.
column8: «Tarjeta» is also the business card: «tarjeta de visita».

column7: What size is the shirt?
column8: For clothes say «talla»; «tamaño» is the size of an object.

column6: Mi color favorito es el azul.
column7: My favourite colour is blue.
column8: It is masculine: «el color»; plural «colores».

column7: I want to buy a gift today.
column8: «Ir de compras» means to go shopping.

column6: Mi tío vende zapatos en el mercado.
column7: My uncle sells shoes at the market.
column8: «Vendedor» is the seller, «venta» the sale.

column7: How much can this shirt cost?
column8: The stem changes: «cuesta» (o→ue).

column7: Today I am wearing a white shirt.
column8: «Llevar» means to take along and to wear.

column7: I am going to try these shoes.
column8: The stem changes: «pruebo» (o→ue).

column7: This coat is too expensive.
column8: Feminine «cara»; «salir caro» means to turn out expensive.

column7: Your shirt is very pretty.
column8: «Bonito» is colloquial and widespread in Latin America; «bello» is more formal.

column7: I want a white shirt.
column8: Colours follow the noun: «una camisa blanca».

column7: My coat is black.
column8: As a colour it agrees with the noun: «una bolsa negra». Said of people, better avoided.

column7: The sea is blue today.
column8: It does not change with gender: «un carro azul, una casa azul».

column7: I like the red shirt.
column8: Red wine is «tinto», but «rojo» for other uses.

column7: The green apple is sour.
column8: «Verde» does not change: «una camisa verde».

column7: I have a lot of work today.
column8: Before an adjective use «muy»: «muy grande».

column7: I have little money today.
column8: Opposite of «mucho»; «un poco» means a little.

column7: I want more bread, please.
column8: Without the accent «mas» means «but» (literary).

column7: Today I spend less money.
column8: Opposite of «más»; «al menos» means «at least».

column7: I do not want to spend much money.
column8: It also means to use up: «gastar energía».

column7: My head hurts today.
column8: «Doler» works like «gustar»: «me duele la cabeza».

column7: I wash my right hand.
column8: It ends in «-o» but is feminine: «la mano».

column7: My left eye hurts.
column8: «Ojo» is also a warning: «¡ojo!» means «watch out!».

column6: Me duele el estómago después de comer.
column7: My stomach hurts after eating.
column8: «Barriga» and «panza» are colloquial words for the belly.

column7: My right foot hurts.
column8: Plural: «pies». «A pie» means «on foot».

column7: My body needs to rest.
column8: «Cuerpo» is also a military or diplomatic corps.

column6: La salud es lo más importante.
column7: Health is the most important thing.
column8: To toast or after a sneeze you say «¡salud!».

column6: El médico trabaja en el hospital.
column7: The doctor works at the hospital.
column8: Feminine: «la médica». You say «ir al médico».

column6: El hospital está lejos de aquí.
column7: The hospital is far from here.
column8: The «h» is silent: «ospital».

column7: I take a medicine every morning.
column8: «Medicina» is also the subject: «estudio medicina».

column6: La farmacia cierra a las diez.
column7: The pharmacy closes at ten.
column8: In Spain pharmacies have a lit-up green cross.

column6: Tengo un dolor en la espalda.
column7: I have a pain in my back.
column8: You say «tener dolor de cabeza» for a headache.

column6: Mi hijo tiene fiebre desde ayer.
column7: My son has had a fever since yesterday.
column8: You say «tener fiebre».

column7: I am very sleepy tonight.
column8: It means both sleep and dream: «tener sueño», «un sueño bonito».

column7: I want to feel the sun today.
column8: «Lo siento» means «I am sorry». For feelings use «sentirse»: «me siento bien».

column6: Me va a doler la espalda mañana.
column7: My back is going to hurt tomorrow.
column8: It takes the indirect object: «me duele», «te duelen los pies».

column7: I need to rest a little today.
column8: «Descanso» is the break or rest.

column7: I must look after my health better.
column8: «¡Cuídate!» is a farewell: «take care».

column7: I am going to take a pill.
column8: In Latin America «tomar» also means «to drink».

column6: Quiero mejorar mi salud este año.
column7: I want to improve my health this year.
column8: «Mejor» is both «better» (adv.) and «better» (adj.).

column7: My son is ill today.
column8: «Estar enfermo» is being ill now; «un enfermo» is a patient.

column7: My grandmother is very strong.
column8: It also applies to sounds: «un ruido fuerte».

column6: Me siento débil después de la fiebre.
column7: I feel weak after the fever.
column8: Opposite of «fuerte».

column6: Estoy muy contento con mi trabajo.
column7: I am very happy with my job.
column8: With «estar»: «estoy contento».

column7: My sister is sad today.
column8: It is used with «estar» for a mood.

column7: I am nervous before the exam.
column8: With «estar» it is a state; with «ser» it is a trait.

column7: Today I sleep very well.
column8: Opposite: «mal». «Muy bien» is «very well».

column7: Today I feel bad.
column8: As an adjective before a masculine noun it becomes «mal»: «mal tiempo».

column7: In the morning I drink tea.
column8: It also means «tomorrow» as an adverb: «mañana voy».

column7: At night I sleep well.
column8: «Buenas noches» is both an evening greeting and good night.

column7: Today is a good day.
column8: It ends in «-a» but is masculine: «el día».

column7: What time is it now?
column8: «¿Qué hora es?» asks the time; «tiempo» is time passing.

column7: I like Latin music.
column8: The stress falls on «mú», hence the written accent.

column7: This song is very pretty.
column8: Plural «canciones»: the written accent disappears.

column7: We watch a film on Saturday.
column8: «Cine» is the cinema and also the genre: «cine mexicano».

column6: Estoy leyendo un libro muy bueno.
column7: I am reading a very good book.
column8: False friend: «librería» is the bookshop, not the library.

column7: My brother plays football.
column8: It is the most popular sport in Latin America and Spain.

column6: El partido empieza a las ocho.
column7: The match starts at eight.
column8: «Partido» is also a political party.

column7: My friend lives in Bogotá.
column8: Feminine: «amiga». «Amigo» is also a friendly form of address.

column6: La fiesta es en mi casa.
column7: The party is at my house.
column8: In Spanish «fiesta» is both a party and a public holiday.

column6: Caminamos por el parque cada tarde.
column7: We walk in the park every afternoon.
column8: Latin American parks often host concerts and small markets.

column6: Mi perro corre por el parque.
column7: My dog runs in the park.
column8: Mind the double «rr»: «perro» (dog) and «pero» (but).

column6: El gato duerme en el sofá.
column7: The cat sleeps on the sofa.
column8: Feminine: «gata». «Gato» is also a car jack in some countries.

column6: Los niños quieren jugar al fútbol.
column7: The children want to play football.
column8: The stem changes: «juego» (u→ue); you say «jugar al fútbol».

column6: Me encanta bailar con mis amigos.
column7: I love dancing with my friends.
column8: «Baile» is the dance; very important in Latin America: salsa, cumbia, tango.

column6: Mi madre canta en la cocina.
column7: My mother sings in the kitchen.
column8: «Cantante» is the singer.

column6: Me gusta escuchar música por la noche.
column7: I like listening to music in the evening.
column8: Not to be confused with «oír» (to hear).

column6: Vamos a mirar una película esta noche.
column7: We are going to watch a film tonight.
column8: «Ver» is to see; «mirar» is to look with attention.

column6: Quiero ver a mis amigos hoy.
column7: I want to see my friends today.
column8: «Nos vemos» is a farewell: «see you».

column6: Me gusta nadar en el mar.
column7: I like swimming in the sea.
column8: «Natación» is swimming as a sport.

column6: Todas las mañanas salgo a correr.
column7: Every morning I go out for a run.
column8: The double «rr» in the middle is strong and rolled.

column7: The party was a lot of fun.
column8: «Divertirse» is to have fun: «me divierto mucho».

column7: This film is very boring.
column8: With «ser» it is boring, with «estar» it is bored.

column6: Mañana estoy libre por la tarde.
column7: Tomorrow I am free in the afternoon.
column8: «Tiempo libre» is free time.

column7: This week I have a lot of work.
column8: The weekend is «el fin de semana».

column7: On Saturday I go to the cinema.
column8: Days of the week are masculine and not capitalised.

column7: On Sundays we eat with the family.
column8: Days are not capitalised: «el domingo», «los domingos».

column7: Today I want to rest at home.
column8: «Hoy en día» means «nowadays».

column6: Ayer vimos una película muy buena.
column7: Yesterday we saw a very good film.
column8: It is used with the past: «ayer fui al cine».

column6: Por la tarde voy al parque.
column7: In the afternoon I go to the park.
column8: «Tarde» is also the adverb «late»: «llegas tarde».

column6: Siempre escucho música por la mañana.
column7: I always listen to music in the morning.
column8: Opposite: «nunca».

column6: Nunca bebo café por la noche.
column7: I never drink coffee at night.
column8: With «nunca» after the verb you need «no»: «no bebo nunca café».

column6: Hola, no hablo muy bien español.
column7: Hello, I do not speak Spanish very well.
column8: The «h» is silent. «Hola» works at any hour and in any setting.

column7: Goodbye, see you tomorrow.
column8: Less final than the Italian «addio»: it is an ordinary farewell.

column7: Thank you very much for your help.
column8: You answer «de nada» or «con gusto» (Latin America).

column6: Un café, por favor, y la cuenta.
column7: A coffee, please, and the bill.
column8: It is used almost every time you ask for something.

column7: My name is Carlos Pérez.
column8: Many Spanish speakers have two surnames: the father's and the mother's.

column6: Mi idioma favorito es el español.
column7: My favourite language is Spanish.
column8: It ends in «-a» but is masculine: «el idioma». «Lengua» is also the tongue.

column7: I speak Spanish with my neighbours.
column8: In Latin America many say «castellano», especially in Argentina and Chile.

column6: Mi jefe habla inglés muy bien.
column7: My boss speaks English very well.
column8: Languages are masculine and not capitalised.

column7: How old are you now?
column8: You say «tener años», like Italian «avere».

column7: Love has no age.
column8: Masculine: «el amor».

column7: Life is very beautiful.
column8: «¡Es la vida!» is a common exclamation.

column7: I do not have much time today.
column8: It means both time and weather: «hace buen tiempo».

column7: I want to see the whole world.
column8: «Todo el mundo» means «everybody».

column7: That man is my uncle.
column8: The «h» is silent.

column6: Mi madre es una mujer fuerte.
column7: My mother is a strong woman.
column8: It can also mean «wife»: «mi mujer». More formal: «esposa».

column6: El niño juega en la calle.
column7: The boy plays in the street.
column8: Feminine «niña». The «ñ» matters.

column6: Soy estudiante y quiero ser doctor.
column7: I am a student and I want to be a doctor.
column8: «Ser» for identity, origin, profession; «estar» for state and location.

column7: I am at home now.
column8: It is for location and state: «estoy en casa», «estoy cansado».

column6: Debes querer mucho a tu familia.
column7: You must love your family very much.
column8: «Te quiero» is «I care about you»; «te amo» is stronger.

column6: Hoy no voy a poder salir.
column7: Today I will not be able to go out.
column8: The stem changes: «puedo» (o→ue).

column7: I want to know the answer today.
column8: «Saber» is to know facts; «conocer» is to know people and places.

column7: I want to meet your family.
column8: With people you add «a»: «conozco a Ana».

column7: I want to learn Spanish quickly.
column8: «Estudiar» is to study; «aprender» is to learn.

column7: I study Spanish every evening.
column8: No preposition needed: «estudio medicina».

column7: I need to understand this new word.
column8: The stem changes: «entiendo» (e→ie).

column7: This word is very difficult.
column8: «Palabra» is also a promise: «tienes mi palabra».

column6: Yo vivo en una ciudad pequeña.
column7: I live in a small city.
column8: The subject pronoun is often dropped: «vivo» is enough.

column7: Do you speak English too?
column8: In Argentina and Central America «vos» is used; «tú» is common elsewhere.

column7: Are you the new boss?
column8: In Latin America «usted» is used with older or unfamiliar people.

column7: We live in the centre.
column8: Feminine: «nosotras».

column7: They work in an office.
column8: Feminine: «ellas». In Latin America «ustedes» is used for «you all».

column7: This book is very interesting.
column8: «Este» is the demonstrative «this».

column6: Mi madre y mi padre viven aquí.
column7: My mother and my father live here.
column8: Before «i-» it becomes «e»: «padre e hijo».

column7: I want to go, but I cannot.
column8: «Pero» (but) and «perro» (dog) differ by the «rr».

column6: No salgo porque estoy cansado hoy.
column7: I am not going out because I am tired today.
column8: «Porque» is the answer; «por qué» (two words) is the question.

column6: Voy al parque con mi perro.
column7: I go to the park with my dog.
column8: «Conmigo» and «contigo» are special forms.

column7: I drink coffee without sugar.
column8: Opposite of «con».

column7: I live in a big city.
column8: A very frequent preposition: «en casa», «en el mar».

column7: My house is very small.
column8: Before adjectives and adverbs: «muy bien»; not with verbs.

column7: My brother also speaks Spanish.
column8: Opposite: «tampoco».

column6: Voy a hacer la cena ahora.
column7: I am going to make dinner now.
column8: Irregular: «hago, haces, hace». «Hace frío» describes the weather.

column6: Mi padre prepara el desayuno hoy.
column7: My father is preparing breakfast today.
column8: «Prepararse» is to get ready: «me preparo para el examen».

column7: Can you say your name again?
column8: Irregular: «digo, dices, dice». «Es decir» means «that is».

column6: Voy a dar un regalo a mi madre.
column7: I am going to give my mother a gift.
column8: Irregular only in the first person: «doy».

column6: Voy a poner la mesa ahora.
column7: I am going to set the table now.
column8: «Poner la mesa» is to set the table; irregular: «pongo».

column7: I need to use the phone now.
column8: «Utilizar» is more formal.

column6: Quiero visitar a mis abuelos pronto.
column7: I want to visit my grandparents soon.
column8: You say «visitar a alguien» (to go and see someone) and «visitar un lugar» (to visit a place).

column6: Puedes entrar por la puerta principal.
column7: You can enter through the main door.
column8: In Latin America «entrar a» is very common; in Spain «entrar en».

column6: Voy a volver a casa temprano.
column7: I am going to come back home early.
column8: The stem changes: «vuelvo» (o→ue); «volver a» + infinitive means «to do again».

column6: Tienes que subir al segundo piso.
column7: You have to go up to the second floor.
column8: Opposite: «bajar». Do not confuse with «salir».

column6: Voy a bajar en la próxima parada.
column7: I am going to get off at the next stop.
column8: «Bajar del autobús» means getting off the bus.

column6: Mi hermano sabe tocar la guitarra.
column7: My brother can play the guitar.
column8: One verb for touching and playing.

column6: Me gusta practicar deporte los sábados.
column7: I like to practise sport on Saturdays.
column8: «Practicar deporte» means doing sport.

column6: Quiero invitar a mis amigos a cenar.
column7: I want to invite my friends to dinner.
column8: «Invitar» can also mean «to treat»: «yo invito».

column6: Tenemos que decidir el precio hoy.
column7: We have to decide on the price today.
column8: «Decidirse» is to make up one's mind.

column6: No quiero olvidar mi llave otra vez.
column7: I do not want to forget my key again.
column8: «Olvidarse de» or «olvidar» without a preposition: «olvidé la llave».

column6: Me gusta compartir la casa con amigos.
column7: I like to share my house with friends.
column8: «Compartir» is to share.

column7: This coffee is very good.
column8: Before a masculine singular noun it becomes «buen»: «un buen día».

column7: The weather is bad today.
column8: Before a masculine singular noun it becomes «mal»: «un mal día».

column7: My brother is very tall.
column8: Opposite: «bajo». For people it is «ser alto».

column7: My boss is very young.
column8: Plural «jóvenes» takes a written accent.

column7: My neighbour is very friendly.
column8: «Simpático» means friendly in manner.

column7: This book is very interesting.
column8: The same in masculine and feminine.

column6: Mi madre es muy feliz aquí.
column7: My mother is very happy here.
column8: Plural «felices»: the «z» becomes «c».

column7: Now I study Spanish at home.
column8: «Ahorita» is a diminutive very common in Mexico: «right now».

column6: Después del trabajo voy al gimnasio.
column7: After work I go to the gym.
column8: With «de»: «después de comer».

column6: Antes de comer me lavo las manos.
column7: Before eating I wash my hands.
column8: With «de»: «antes de comer».

column6: Ya tengo mi billete de tren.
column7: I already have my train ticket.
column8: «Ya» has many uses: «ya voy», «ya no».

column7: I am not hungry yet.
column8: Synonym: «aún».

column7: He works at a school.
column8: With the accent «él» is the pronoun; «el» without it is the article.

column7: She lives in Buenos Aires.
column8: The «ll» is pronounced like «y» across most of Latin America.

column7: I want to eat something tasty now.
column8: Opposite: «nada».

column6: No tengo nada en la mochila.
column7: I have nothing in my backpack.
column8: After the verb you need «no»: «no tengo nada».

column7: I am from a small city.
column8: «De» shows origin and possession: «el libro de Ana».

column6: Voy a la oficina en autobús.
column7: I go to the office by bus.
column8: Before a direct-object person: «veo a mi madre».

column7: Do you want tea or coffee now?
column8: Before «o-» it becomes «u»: «siete u ocho».

column7: When I arrive, I prepare dinner.
column8: With the accent «¿cuándo?» is the question.

column7: My birthday is in December.
column8: Unchanged in the plural: «dos cumpleaños».
